beats.text: Opening the same programs. Moving the same windows. Typing the same text, again. {kd}K-Desktop does it for you, with a {key}key, a {menu}menu, or your {voice}voice.
In the next few minutes: {get}get it running, take a {tour}quick tour, and make your {first}first command.
K-Desktop is a {single}single portable program for {windows}Windows 10 and 11. On its {github}GitHub page, open {releases}Releases, and download {exe}KDesktop.exe.
There's {noinstall}no installer, and nothing else to install. Put it in a {folder}folder of your own, and {open}open it.
If Windows {smart}SmartScreen steps in, choose {more}More info, then {anyway}Run anyway.

From then on, it {keeps}keeps itself up to date. When there's a {new}new version, it downloads it and {restarts}restarts while you're not using it, in a couple of seconds. In {settings}Settings, Updates, you can have it {tell}just tell you instead.
The first time, a short {welcome}welcome sets up the basics.
Pick a {theme}theme: light, dark, or the same as Windows. And a {language}language: English, Spanish, French, German or Italian.
Next, {what}what it can do, at a glance.
{startup}Start with Windows comes on, so your hotkeys always work. It starts with {admin}administrator rights, without asking every time.
Choose a key for the {launcher}launcher, and one to {show}bring up K-Desktop from anywhere.
Closing the window doesn't close K-Desktop. It keeps working from its {tray}icon next to the clock.
{voice}Voice and {assistants}assistants are optional, so you can leave them for later. And you're {done}all set.
Now, a quick look around the panel.

{commands}Commands are the heart of it: actions you start with a hotkey. {events}Events run them for you, when something happens on your PC. And the {quickmenu}QuickMenu puts them in a menu, right under your mouse.

{kboard}K-Board changes what your keys do. {macros}Macros record what you do, and play it back. {texts}Texts swaps a short abbreviation for a long text. And {layouts}Layouts remembers where your windows go.

{assistant}Assistant is home to optional characters you can talk to. The {agenda}Agenda keeps your appointments. {history}History lists everything that ran. {settings}Settings are grouped by topic, and {search}searchable with Control F. And along the way, you'll unlock {achievements}achievements.
And your {phone}phone can be a remote, with the web app or the Android app. Each of these has its own short video.
Time for your first command. In {commands}Commands, click {new}New command, and call it {name}Notepad.
Add a hotkey. Press {ctrl}Control, {alt}Alt, {n}N.
Then an {add}action: {run}Run application, {notepad}Notepad. It even picks up the program's {icon}icon by itself.
Click {run}Run to try it. Now, from {anywhere}anywhere, press {ctrl}Control, {alt}Alt, {n}N... and {there}there it is.
One last tip. A hotkey doesn't have to be a key. It can be a {mouse}mouse button, a {corner}corner of the screen, or a {gesture}mouse gesture.
Next up: {next}commands, actions and hotkeys, in depth.
Thanks for watching.
